phonemes.desc: Initial sound of Rꜥ, as attested in the egyptian tradition.
Subsequent syllables preserve the name's inherited shape.

pronunciation.note: Rꜥ is Tier 2 because its Unicode restoration preserves the orthographic signature appropriate to the egyptian tradition.

domains.title: Sun, Creation, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Rꜥ
domains.lead: In the egyptian tradition, Rꜥ governed sun, creation, kingship. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.title: Primary Sphere
cards.body: Rꜥ is principally associated with sun, creation, kingship.

cards.title: Cultural Role
cards.body: Worshippers approached Rꜥ through cult, myth, and the material culture of the egyptian world.

symbols.meaning: Material focus of devotion for Rꜥ

symbols.name: Ankh
symbols.meaning: Symbol of life and divine power

mythology.lead: The myths of Rꜥ preserve the name's power and personality across generations of retelling.

myths.title: The story of Rꜥ
myths.text: Rꜥ appears in egyptian tradition as a figure whose domain over sun, creation, kingship shapes both cosmic order and human experience. The surviving narratives emphasize Rꜥ's role, attributes, and relationships with other powers.

lore.syncretism: Egyptian deities were syncretized with one another and, in the Greco-Roman period, with Greek and Roman gods; temple theology developed complex composite forms.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name survives in Egyptological scholarship, museum collections, modern spirituality, and the global fascination with Pharaonic civilization. Restoring Rꜥ in Unicode preserves the name's cultural specificity against the flattening force of plain ASCII.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Rꜥ carries within it a egyptian understanding of sun (from egyptian rꜥ). Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form.
sources: The Pyramid Texts; The Coffin Texts; The Book of the Dead.
Beekes, R. S. P. Etymological Dictionary of Greek. Leiden: Brill, 2010.
Egyptian material evidence includes temple reliefs, statuary, papyri, amulets, and tomb inscriptions from the Pharaonic through Ptolemaic periods.
